text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Selkirk v. Swain,

2016 BCSC 1454

Date: 20160808

Docket:
14-3752

Registry: Victoria

Between:

John Selkirk

Plaintiff

And:

Harry Swain, Mitchell Krieger, Tania Miller, April-Dawn Best, Trudi
Brown,

Brian Butler, Ethne Cullen, Jim Hesser, Patricia Lortie, Margo Northey,

Michael Warren, Barry Mungham, Sheila Protti, Terry Scandrett, Marcia

McNeil, Natexa Verbrugge, Victoria Symphony Foundation

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice J. A. Power

Reasons for Judgment

Appearing in Person:

J.
Selkirk

Counsel for the Defendants:

A.
R. Westmacott, Q.C.

Counsel for the Defendant Marcia McNeil:

P.M.J.
Arvisais

Place and Date of Trial/Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

May
24 and 25, 2016

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

August 8, 2016

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The background of this case is aptly summarized
in one of the arbitration decisions referenced in the Chambers materials in
this case,
Musicians’ Assn. of Victoria and the Islands, Local 247, AFM v.
Victoria Symphony Society (Selkirk Grievance)
, [2012] B.C.C.A.A.A. No. 109
at para 1:

[1]        This
is an unhappy situation.  After twenty-five years as a Full Contract Symphony
Musician with the employer, Principal Trumpet John Selkirk suffered [a]
work-related auditory injury in 2008 that resulted in a permanent hearing
disability which prevented him from continuing as a musician with the Symphony.
He has not played with the Symphony since March 2008.

[
2
]

As I will outline, there is a long history to this
dispute that has carried on through arbitration, WorkSafeBC, and in this court
relating to the plaintiff’s dismissal from the Victoria Symphony.

[
3
]

This decision concerns two applications brought
by the defendants seeking an order to strike the plaintiff’s notice of civil
claim and dismiss the action.

[
4
]

I have decided that I should accede to those applications.
My reasons are as follows.

PARTIES

[
5
]

Since there are a number of parties referenced
in the style of cause, I will set them out here.

[
6
]

The plaintiff was a musician with the Victoria
Symphony from 1983 until 2009.

[
7
]

The defendant Victoria Symphony Foundation
(“VSF”) is a registered charitable foundation which raises money and manages an
endowment to support the Victoria Symphony Society (the “VSS”).  The VSS is the
non-profit society which conducts the Victoria Symphony Orchestra.  The VSS is
not named as a defendant in this action, although it was named in a previous
action.

[
8
]

The defendant Harry Swain is a board member of
the VSF and was the president of the board of directors of the VSS at the
material time.  The defendant Trudi Brown is a current VSF board member and was
a VSS board member at the material time.  Brian Butler is a current VSF and VSS
board member, but was not a VSS board member at the material time.  The
defendant Natexa Verbrugge was a VSS board member at the material time and was
the VSS’s nominee on the arbitration panel.

[
9
]

The defendants Mitchell Krieger and Tania Miller
are staff of the VSS.  Mitchell Krieger is the executive director and Tania Miller
is the musical director.

[
10
]

The defendant Marcia McNeil was legal counsel
for the VSS at the material time.

[
11
]

I also note that prior to this application a
notice of discontinuance was filed by the plaintiff discontinuing the action
against the following defendants:  April Dawn Best, Ethne Cullen, Jim Hesser,
Patricia Lortie, Barry Mungham, Margo Northey, Sheila Protti, Terry Scandrett,
and Michael Warren.

BACKGROUND

[
12
]

As I have noted, from 1983 until 2009, the
plaintiff was a musician with the Victoria Symphony Orchestra.  He occupied the
position of principal trumpet.

[
13
]

As a musician with the VSS, he was a member of
the Musicians’ Association of Victoria and the Islands, Local 247 (the “union”).
The VSS had voluntarily recognized the union as the bargaining agent for its
members.  All musicians had personal contracts with the VSS that were made
pursuant to a master agreement between the union and the VSS.

[
14
]

Full concert musicians, such as the plaintiff,
had their contracts renewed annually as part of the master agreement.

[
15
]

In early 2008, the plaintiff sustained a hearing
injury while playing in the symphony.  The plaintiff, after taking a number of
sick days, eventually made a claim under WorkSafeBC and went on medical leave.

[
16
]

Leading up to this time and during it, it is
clear from the evidence that the relationships between the plaintiff and the
VSS began to breakdown.  There were artistic differences between the plaintiff
and Tania Miller, who is the musical director of the VSS.  As well, there were
disagreements between the plaintiff and Michael Krieger, who is the executive
director of the VSS, over the medical information that was to be provided to
the VSS and when the plaintiff would be returning to work.

[
17
]

By August 13, 2009, the plaintiff had signed his
annual contract and says that he intended to return to work for the 2009/10
symphony season.  He says that he received permission from his audiologist to
return to work, but that he had not received clearance from WorkSafeBC.

[
18
]

However, on September 9, 2009, the VSS issued
notice to the plaintiff that his contract had been dismissed for cause for
failing to provide the VSS with information about his illness and his prospects
of returning to work.

[
19
]

On September 17, 2009, the union filed a
grievance on behalf of the plaintiff which alleged that he had been dismissed
without just cause and sought to have his position reinstated.

[
20
]

In February 2010, the plaintiff filed the first
wrongful dismissal application in this court against the VSS, but chose to
discontinue that action in favour of pursuing his grievance.

[
21
]

In September 2011, the plaintiff filed a second
wrongful dismissal application in this court against the VSS, but chose not to actively
pursue the action while the grievance process was unfolding.

[
22
]

The grievance process was eventually heard by an
arbitration panel consisting of arbitrator Jim Dorsey Q.C., employer
representative Natexa Verbrugge, and union representative Jim Lamb.  The panel
convened a hearing on April 17 to 19, 2012.

[
23
]

On May 11, 2012, the arbitration panel rendered
its decision cited as
Musicians’ Assn. of Victoria and the Islands, Local
247, AFM v. Victoria Symphony Society (Selkirk Grievance)
, [2012]
B.C.C.A.A.A. No 66.  They held that the VSS had dismissed the plaintiff without
just cause.  The panel found that the dismissal was premature, that the
plaintiff was entitled to be on sick leave and that the VSS acted prematurely
as the plaintiff had informed them that he had signed his contract and wished
to meet with them regarding the upcoming season.  However, the panel also found
that the plaintiff could not be reinstated to his former position due to a
permanent disability.

[
24
]

The VSS and the union were not able to resolve
the appropriate remedy and a further decision of the arbitration panel was
issued on August 9, 2012, ordering the VSS to pay the plaintiff $18,000 set off
by $4,104.10 owed to the VSS as an overpayment of benefits.  The arbitration
panel found that there was no manner in which Mr. Selkirk could be re-instated
to a non-musical role with the symphony.  That decision was cited in para.1 of
these reasons.

[
25
]

The money was paid and neither of the
arbitration panels’ decisions was appealed.

[
26
]

The plaintiff then commenced a claim before the
Labour Relations Board (“LRB”), pursuant to
s. 12
of the
Labour Relations
Code
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 244, alleging that his union had breached its duty
of fair representation.

[
27
]

On April 18, 2013, the LRB dismissed the
plaintiff’s claim against the union.  In finding that the union had not
breached its duty of fair representation, the LRB held that the decision to not
submit the medical reports was a reasonable tactical decision:

[54]      In the case at hand, I find that
the Union’s decision not to enter the 2011 Report into evidence (in exchange
for the Employer’s agreement not to put the Civil Pleadings before the
Arbitration Board) demonstrates a reasonable and rational connection to the
relevant considerations at hand, namely, returning Selkirk to employment.  The
Union concluded that the prospect of the Civil Pleadings being entered into
evidence would have ended any reasonable chance of reinstatement as it would
have further demonstrated that the employment relationship was broken.  (Indeed,
even without the Civil Proceedings in evidence, the Arbitration Board found
that the requisite trust was not present to allow reinstatement into any
position.)  Furthermore, the Union also took into account the possibility that
the 2011 report would have been of little value at all given the absence of any
evidence to show a continuous employment relationship between 2009 and 2011.

…

[56]      The
task before this Panel is to determine whether the Union made a reasoned
decision to exclude the 2011 Report from evidence before the Arbitration Board.
I find that it did.  The Union’s representatives turned their minds to the
issues and provided reasons for their actions (
Chicione
at para. 27).
The Union’s decision was rationally connected to relevant consideration of
returning Selkirk to employment.  As such, I also find that there is no
evidence the Union acted with blatant or reckless disregard for Selkirk’s
interest.

[
28
]

The plaintiff then applied under
s. 141
of the
Labour
Relations

Code
for leave and reconsideration of the decision;
however, the LRB did not grant leave citing that the application “did not
disclose a good, arguable case of reviewable error.”

[
29
]

In 2013, following the decisions of the LRB, the
plaintiff began to pursue the second civil action against the VSS in this
court; however, that action was dismissed by Justice Leask on August 27, 2013.  Oral
reasons were given and they were not before me on this application.

[
30
]

In 2014, the plaintiff filed a human rights
complaint against the VSS; however, that complaint was not accepted as it was
past the limitation date.

[
31
]

In October 2014, the plaintiff filed this
action.

POSITION OF THE PARTIES

[
32
]

The defendants say the notice of civil claim
should be struck and the claim dismissed against the VSF and the foundation’s
directors because there is no cause of action under Rule 9-5(1)(a), the claims
are frivolous and vexatious under Rule 9‑5(1)(b), the claims are an
abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d) and the claims fail to disclose a
bona
fide
triable issue under Rule 9-6(4).  They argue the VSF and its directors
did not have a contractual relationship with the plaintiff nor were the VFS or
its directors responsible for the administration or management of the VSS or
its employment relationships.

[
33
]

The defendants also argue that the notice of
civil claim should be struck and the claim dismissed against the defendant
directors of the VSS and the defendant staff members of the VSS because the
claims are frivolous and vexatious under Rule 9-5(1)(b) and an abuse of process
under Rule 9-5(1)(d) and fail to disclose a
bona fide
triable issue
under Rule 9-6(4).  They say this because the claims are a collateral attack on
the legitimate arbitration process which already ruled on the grievance.  They
argue that any new claims should have been pursued under the grievance process
of the collective agreement or would be barred by the limitation period.

[
34
]

The defendant, Ms. McNeil, argues that the
claims against her should be dismissed pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d).
She submits that at all material times she acted within the confines of her
role as solicitor for the VSS.

[
35
]

The plaintiff, who is self-represented,
acknowledged in his submissions that he had challenges articulating his cause
of action in both his pleadings and in his oral argument.  He was assisted by a
friend during the hearing.  I am of the view that the defendants, in their
submissions, have fairly characterized his arguments.  It is evident that the
plaintiff alleges that a variety of employment-related wrongs were committed
against him while he was a member of the Victoria Symphony Orchestra.  He
alleges that harassment took place.  He also alleges that the VSS erred in the
way they characterized the employment relationship between the symphony and the
musicians, which caused tax consequences for him.  He argues that the VSS,
throughout the arbitration process, damaged the plaintiff by not allowing him
to return as a musician despite the plaintiff being healthy to do so.

[
36
]

Much of the plaintiff’s cause of action and
arguments on this application focus on why an audiologist report was not
admitted to the arbitration panel for consideration.  He says that the
arbitration panel made its findings, that he was permanently disabled and not
able to return to work at the symphony, based on misleading information.  Part
of his notice of civil claim is that he says both the union and the employer
were complicit in having the panel make its decision based on inaccurate
information.  He argues that this amounts to negligence and fraud and that he
should be compensated because the defendants were complicit in having the panel
receive what he calls misleading information.

[
37
]

He also says that the manner in which he was
dismissed defamed him and he should be compensated by the VSS for destroying
his career.

[
38
]

The plaintiff’s argument in this application is
essentially that the collective agreement and the grievance process generally
lacked the jurisdiction to hear the complaint and as a result the plaintiff
should be permitted to bring his claims to this court.  He attacks the
legitimacy of the collective agreement and says that he was an independent
contractor and not within the jurisdiction of the LRB.  He also has concerns
with the manner in which the grievance process was conducted and wishes to
bring these concerns to this court.

[
39
]

The defendants deny these claims and say that
the plaintiff already had the opportunity to raise these claims in the
grievance process, which was the correct forum for him to do so.  They argue
that all of the issues raised in the pleadings were arbitral issues.

THE LAW

[
40
]

The defendants make their application under
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
9‑5(1)(a), (b) and (d) and 9-6(4).  Rule 9-5
provides:

(1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)        it
is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it
may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding,
or

(d)        it
is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
41
]

In considering whether or not a claim discloses
no reasonable claim or defence under Rule 9-5(1)(a), the test is whether,
assuming the facts in the notice of civil claim to be true, it is “plain and
obvious” that the plaintiff’s case discloses no reasonable cause of action and
is destined to fail.  If the plaintiff’s case might succeed, he should have his
day in court regardless of the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty
of the case, and notwithstanding the potential of the defendants to present a
strong defence (
Young v. Borzoni et al,
2007 BCCA 16
).

[
42
]

A court may also strike a notice of civil claim
and dismiss the case under Rule 9-5(1)(b) if the claim is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious.  These terms have been described in
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No.
2160 (S.C.) as follows:

[46]      The authorities provide little
guidance as to what constitutes pleadings that are “unnecessary”, “scandalous”,
“frivolous” or “embarrassing”.  However some principles do emerge.

[47]      Irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.).  An “embarrassing”
and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it will involve the
parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the action by
involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas Hotels
Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.).  An allegation which is
scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the proceedings.  It will
only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College of Dental
Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.).  A pleading
is “unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to establishing the
plaintiff's cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts
v. Harrigan
,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.).  A pleading that is
superfluous will not be struck out if it is not necessarily unnecessary or
otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v. Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber Co.

(1920), 28 B.C.R 39 (C.A.)
.  A pleading is “frivolous” if it is obviously
unsustainable, not in the sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because
of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.
,
[1992]
B.C.J. No. 1567
, (6 July 1992), Prince George Registry 20714 (B.C.S.C.).

[
43
]

The doctrine of issue estoppel exists to prevent
parties from re-litigating questions that could have been raised at earlier
proceedings.  Madam Justice E.A. Arnold-Bailey in
Rivet v. British Columbia
,

2007 BCSC 731
at para.
83
, explained that “[the] doctrine prevents a party from
re-litigating matters by simply relying upon a different theory of liability or
placing a different ‘spin’ on the same set of facts.”  In order for the
doctrine of issue estoppel to apply, the applicant must show that:

(a)        the same question has been
decided in a previous proceeding;

(b)        the earlier decision was final;

(c)        the parties,
or their privies, were the same in both proceedings.

British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation
Board v. Figliola
,
2011 SCC 52 (CanLII)
, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 422 at para.
27
.

[
44
]

Issue estoppel is an equitable remedy designed
to prevent injustices and must be used to achieve fairness according to the
circumstances of each case (
Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc.
,

2001 SCC 44 (CanLII)
, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 460 at para.
63
).

[
45
]

However, the Supreme Court of Canada has held
that even where issue estoppel is not strictly available, the doctrine of abuse
of process can be triggered when allowing the litigation to proceed would
violate principles such as “judicial economy, consistency, finality and the
integrity of the administration of justice” (
Figliola
at para.
33
).

[
46
]

Under Rule 9-5(1)(d) a court may strike a
pleading and dismiss a claim if the claim is an abuse of process.  The Supreme
Court of Canada has said that the doctrine of abuse of process is part of the
inherent power of the courts designed to prevent the misuse of the courts:
Toronto
(City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 77.  Justice Arbour explained
the doctrine of abuse of process and its related policy foundations as follows:

[37]      In the context that interests us
here, the doctrine of abuse of process engages “the inherent power of the court
to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would ... bring the
administration of justice into disrepute” (
Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles

(2000),
2000 CanLII 8514 (ON CA)
, 51 O.R. (3d) 481    (C.A.), at para.
55
, per
Goudge J.A., dissenting (approved [2002] 3 S.C.R. 307,
2002 SCC 63 (CanLII)
)).
Goudge J.A. expanded on that concept in the following terms at paras. 55-56:

The
doctrine of abuse of process engages the inherent power of the court to prevent
the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a
party to the litigation before it or would in some other way bring the
administration of justice into disrepute.
It is a flexible doctrine
unencumbered by the specific requirements of concepts such as issue estoppel.

See
House of Spring Gardens Ltd. v. Waite,

[1990] 3 W.L.R. 347 at p.
358, [1990] 2 All E.R. 990 (C.A.)
.

One
circumstance in which abuse of process has been applied is where the litigation
before the court is found to be in essence an attempt to relitigate a claim
which the court has already determined
.

[emphasis added]

[
47
]

Rule 9-6(4) provides:

(4)        In an
action, an answering party may, after serving a responding pleading on a
claiming party, apply under this rule for judgment dismissing all or part of a
claim in the claiming party's originating pleading.

[
48
]

The application of Rule 9-6 prevents claims that
have no chance of success from proceeding to trial.  Whereas Rule 9-5(1)
considers whether the claims are deficient as a matter of law, Rule 9-6(4) is
appropriate in cases where the plaintiff is bound to lose based on the facts:  see

Drummond v. Moore
,
2012 BCSC 496
at para.
25
.

DISCUSSION

[
49
]

The VSF is a separate legal entity than the VSS.
It is a registered charitable foundation which raises money and manages an endowment
to support the VSS.  Neither the VSF, not its directors, had any contractual
relations with the plaintiff nor were they responsible for the administration
or management of the VSS.  Furthermore, the VSF is not vicariously liable for
the acts of the VSS as they do not have the requite control over the actions of
the symphony to warrant that relationship:  see
Speckling v. Kearney et al
,

2006 BCSC 506
, aff’d
2007 BCCA 145
.

[
50
]

In my view, it is plain and obvious that the
plaintiff’s case discloses no reasonable cause of action against the VSF or its
directors and that the claims against them are destined to fail.

[
51
]

Of the remaining defendants, the claims against
Harry Swain, Trudi Brown, Brian Butler, and Natexa Verbrugge are based on their
roles as directors of the VSS during the material time and against Mitchell
Krieger and Tania Miller as staff of the VSS at the time.

[
52
]

The plaintiff’s pleadings are difficult to
decipher; however, the plaintiff makes a number of arguments to suggest that
the grievance and arbitration process was flawed or lacked legitimacy, which he
says allows him to make these arguments in this court.

[
53
]

He says that he was an independent contractor
(rather than a dependant contractor) and that because of this the collective
agreement did not apply to him.  He also says that the collective agreement in
general was designed to avoid source income tax deductions and that the union
had no authority over him because it was not certified by the LRB.  He also
suggests that the LRB does not have the exclusive jurisdiction to decide on
issues.

[
54
]

Section 139 of the
Code
gives exclusive
jurisdiction to the LRB to decide certain questions.  The section explicitly
provides that:

The board has exclusive jurisdiction to
decide a question arising under this Code and on application by any person or
on its own motion may decide for all purposes of this Code any question,
including, without limitation, any question as to whether

(a)        a
person is an employer or employee,

(b)        an
organization or association is an employers' organization or a trade union,

(c)        a
collective agreement has been entered into,

(d)        a
person is or what persons are bound by a collective agreement,

(e)        a
person is or what persons are parties to a collective agreement,

(f)        a
collective agreement has been entered into on behalf of a person,

(g)        a
collective agreement is in full force and effect,

(h)        a
person is bargaining collectively or has bargained collectively in good faith,

…

(k)        a
person is a member in good standing of a trade union,

…

(n)        a
person is a dependent contractor,

…

(r)        a
trade union, council of trade unions or employers' organization is fulfilling a
duty of fair representation,

…

[
55
]

If the plaintiff had concerns regarding whether
or not the collective agreement was valid, whether he was a dependent
contractor, or whether he was bound by the collective agreement process, he was
obliged to take these questions to the LRB for determination.

[
56
]

However, the plaintiff acceded to the
jurisdiction of the grievance process and was ultimately partially successful
in the outcome of the arbitration process.  He was awarded damages to
compensate him for the VSS’s decision to terminate his contract prematurely.

[
57
]

I note that paras. 3 and 4 of the first arbitration
decision dated May 11, 2012 state:

[3]        The union and the employer agree
this arbitration board is properly constituted to finally decide the merits of
the union’s grievance under their collective agreement and the
Labour
Relations Code
.

[4]        Mr.
Selkirk was covered by the Master Agreement between the union and employer and
employed during the September to May season to attend and perform services
under a personal contract.  He was one of two Trumpets among the 34 and 23
designated part contract musicians with the employer.  Full contract musicians
do freelance work during and between seasons and have a choice whether they
will contract with the Symphony for any sessions between seasons.

[
58
]

The plaintiff, who was represented by legal
counsel at the time, did not appeal the findings of the arbitration panel or
seek a judicial review of the decision based on any procedural deficiencies.  As
noted above, he did challenge whether or not his union had breached their duty
of fair representation, but the LRB ultimately concluded that the union did not
breach its duty.  Furthermore, the plaintiff also filed a civil claim alleging
similar claims against the VSS, but that claim was dismissed by Judge Leask.

[
59
]

I conclude that the claims made against the
former directors and staff of the VSS are barred by the doctrine of issue
estoppel.  The plaintiff’s action raises the same questions that were in issue
or could have been raised as issues before the arbitration panel:  whether the
VSS was allowed to terminate the contract, what the appropriate remedy should
be, and whether the contract came within the jurisdiction of the grievance
process.  The arbitration panel’s decision was final as no appeals were made.  The
mutuality requirement is made out because the claims against the defendants are
made as a result of their capacity as VSS directors and staff and as a result
they are “privies” of the VSS.  On that basis I would find that the claim is
frivolous because it is barred by the doctrine of issue estoppel.

[
60
]

However, if I am wrong I would also decide the
application on the basis that the claim is an abuse of process.  It is an abuse
of process for the plaintiff to attack the jurisdiction of the grievance
process, the procedure that was adhered to, and the results of the arbitration
board in this forum.  The plaintiff may have had opportunities to appeal the
results or judicially review the decisions in their appropriate forum; however,
that was not done.  The plaintiff is attempting to undermine the grievance
process, which he participated in and was partially successful, and to
relitigate the issues.  The claims he makes deal with complaints that have
already been determined or that should have been raised during the grievance
and arbitration process.

[
61
]

The records show that as far as the parties were
concerned, the grievance and arbitration process was properly constituted and
the outcome fairly determined.  If the plaintiff wishes to challenge either the
results of the arbitration panel or the process adhered to that should be
through an appeal or through the judicial review mechanisms that are intended
by the legislature (see
Figliola

at 34).  To allow the plaintiff to
re-try the case and circumvent the findings of the arbitration board would
undermine confidence in the justice system, and the fairness and integrity of
the arbitration process.  It would potentially create inconsistent results,
unnecessarily duplicative proceedings, and it would undermine the finality of a
decision and process which the parties should have been able to rely on.

[
62
]

Similarly, the issues concerning whether the audiologist
report should have been admitted during the grievance process was already
adjudicated by the LRB and leave to reconsider this decision was denied.  The
LRB found that the plaintiff’s own representative had made a tactical decision
to omit the report.  To reconsider these issues could potentially create
inconsistent results, undermine the labour relations process, and exhaust judicial
and party resources.

[
63
]

Furthermore, to the extent that any new issues
have been raised by the plaintiff in this case, such as whether the defendants
engaged in unlawful business practices, harassed the plaintiff, threatened to
terminate the plaintiff, or damaged the plaintiff’s reputation by the way they
conducted their business, I find that those are arbitral issues that could and
should have been raised by the plaintiff in the collective agreement’s
grievance procedure.

[
64
]

The plaintiff suggests that this court should
allow the plaintiff to proceed because it is in the interests of justice to do
so, and because as a self-represented litigant he has been denied access to
justice.  However, I note that the plaintiff has had ample access to address
his concerns through the grievance process and through the administrative
process under the
Code
, and through previous court proceedings.  The
need for the plaintiff to have access to justice is also balanced with the defendants’
right to avoiding unnecessary relitigation and unnecessary expenditure of
resources and to be able to rely on the finality of the arbitration process.

[
65
]

The defendant Marcia McNeil adopts the position
of the other defendants that the claim should be dismissed.  She further
submits that no action can exist against a solicitor for the actions of her
client, in which she has not participated.  Furthermore, no action lies against
the solicitor unless she is alleged to have somehow stepped outside of her role
as counsel and undertaken some sort of obligation to the plaintiff.  Those
allegations have not been made in this claim.

[
66
]

The plaintiff argues that, despite knowing its
contents, Ms. McNeil withheld the 2011 medical report from the arbitration
board and as a result she withheld or suppressed evidence of medical fact.  Counsel
for Ms. McNeil pointed out, however, that the plaintiff was in possession of
the report and that it was a tactical decision by his union not to adduce the
report into evidence.  Ms. McNeil was under no obligation to present the
plaintiff’s case on his behalf and owed no duty to the plaintiff.

[
67
]

I would find that it is plain and obvious that
the plaintiff has disclosed no cause of action against Ms. McNeil.

CONCLUSION

[
68
]

As I noted at the beginning, this is an unhappy
situation.  It is regrettable that after 25 years of employment with the
symphony, and the process that followed, the plaintiff, Mr. Selkirk, continues
to feel aggrieved.  However, the issues raised by Mr. Selkirk are arbitral
issues that could have been, and largely were dealt with, through the grievance
process in this action.

[
69
]

In the result, the plaintiff’s notice of civil claim
is struck.

[
70
]

The defendants were successful in this
application and are entitled to their costs at Scale B.

“J.
A. Power, J.”

The
Honourable Madam Justice J. A. Power
